etymology: From the strategy credited to the campaign strategist Lynton Crosby: to end an argument you are losing, put a dead cat on the table.
trigger: A story that will not stop, and a week that needs a different one.
tell: Something outrageous appears at eight in the morning, unrelated to the story it replaced, and the people who were answering questions stop answering them.
counter: Name the cat. Keep asking the original question, on the record, until the answer is on the record too.

confused_with.tell: The slopagandist drowns the zone in volume; the dead cat changes the subject with one loud object.

senses: The move of putting something so shocking on the table that the conversation has to be about it: the story you were asked about is replaced by the thing nobody can stop looking at.

It works because attention is finite and news is a queue. Coverage can only hold one thing at a time, so the object does not have to be relevant - it only has to be louder, and the agenda moves while the question stays unanswered. What changed was never the facts; it was what everyone was looking at.
example: *"The contract story was finally landing, and then a **dead cat** hit the table at eight in the morning - by noon nobody could remember what the contract said."*
